topic: Final boss: library internals & build your own

questions.question: Why should an app share one OkHttpClient and use `client.newBuilder()` for variants, instead of creating a new client for each request?
options: Each client has its own connection pool and dispatcher threads; sharing reuses warm connections and resources
OkHttpClient is a singleton under the hood, so extra instances are discarded and their settings are ignored
Only the first client created in a process can use HTTP/2, so later clients fall back to HTTP/1.1
A new client must do a fresh DNS lookup and TLS handshake for each request, even to the same host
questions.explanation: Connection pooling (keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing) is a large part of OkHttp's performance, and it only works when calls share a client. `newBuilder()` creates a client with different timeouts or interceptors that still shares the same pool and dispatcher. Each separate client wastes memory and threads and pays handshake costs again.

questions.question: Retrofit creates the implementation of an API interface at runtime with a `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, parsing each method's annotations once into a cached request factory.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `retrofit.create()` returns a dynamic proxy; on the first call to a method, Retrofit reads its annotations and parameter types into a ServiceMethod and caches it. Later calls reuse it, so the reflection cost is paid once per method. This reflection is also why Retrofit interfaces need R8 keep rules (shipped with the library).

questions.question: You build your own image loader with a memory cache. What must the memory cache key include?
options: The URL plus the view's identity, so every ImageView or cell gets its own separate cached bitmap
Only the URL, since the same URL always gives the same pixels no matter where the image is shown
The source (URL or URI) plus the requested size and any transformations applied to the decoded bitmap
A hash of the downloaded file bytes, so that two URLs with the same file share a single bitmap
questions.explanation: The memory cache stores decoded results, so a 100px circle-cropped thumbnail and a full-screen version of the same URL are different entries; keying by URL alone hands out the wrong size or shape. Coil and Glide build keys this way. Keying by view prevents reuse across cells, and hashing bytes means downloading before you can check the cache.

questions.question: Room enables SQLite write-ahead logging (WAL) by default on most devices. What does WAL give you?
options: Every write is fully durable without fsync, so commits get faster and power loss can never lose data
Queries are moved to a separate process, so a slow query can no longer block the app's main thread
Several writers can commit at the same moment, as long as each of them writes to a different table
Readers can keep reading while a write is in progress, though there is still only one writer at a time
questions.explanation: With WAL, writes go to a separate log file, so readers can see a consistent snapshot of the main database without waiting for the writer. SQLite still allows one writer at a time across the whole database. Room uses a pool of reader connections plus one writer connection for this; it does not make queries safe to run on the main thread.

questions.question: You are writing your own HTTP response cache (or checking how OkHttp's works). Which behaviours are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Expect a 304 response to include the full body again, so you can check it against the cached copy
Store the ETag / Last-Modified and send If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since when revalidating
Cache POST responses by URL, so that repeating the same POST can be served from the cache
Respect Cache-Control directives such as max-age, no-cache and no-store from the server
On 304 Not Modified, reuse the cached body and update the stored headers from the 304 response
questions.explanation: Conditional requests let the server answer 'still valid' cheaply, and the client merges the 304's headers into its cached entry. Cache-Control is the contract that decides freshness and whether storing is allowed. POST is not cacheable by URL in practice because it is not idempotent and the body matters; a 304 has no body by definition.

questions.question: In Media3 ExoPlayer, what is the rule about which thread you may call the player from?
options: Any thread may call the player at any time, because every public method is synchronised internally
Call it only from its application thread (the looper it was created on, usually main); heavy playback work runs internally on its own thread
Calls must come from the decoder thread, which you get with `player.getPlaybackLooper()` before use
All calls must come from a background thread, since calling the player on the main thread causes an ANR
questions.explanation: ExoPlayer is not thread-safe for app calls: it must be accessed from a single application thread (the looper passed or the one it was built on), and listener callbacks arrive there too. Loading, buffering and rendering happen on an internal playback thread, so main-thread calls are cheap. Calling it from random threads leads to errors and undefined state.

questions.question: When talking HTTP/2 to a host, OkHttp still opens one TCP connection per in-flight request to that host, just as with HTTP/1.1.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent streams over one connection, and OkHttp's ConnectionPool reuses that single connection for parallel calls to the same host. HTTP/1.1 needs a separate connection for each concurrent request because each connection handles one request-response at a time. This is a major reason to share a single client.

questions.question: A binding is missing from the dependency graph. How does that failure show up with Dagger/Hilt compared with Koin?
options: Both fail at build time, because Koin also generates a factory class for every definition during compilation
Both fail at runtime, because Dagger/Hilt also look up bindings with reflection when the app starts
Dagger/Hilt fail at runtime on first injection, while Koin checks every module while the app is starting up
Dagger/Hilt fail the build when generating code; Koin fails at runtime on first resolution, unless a test runs `verify()` / checkModules
questions.explanation: Dagger builds the whole graph during annotation processing (KSP/kapt), so a missing binding is a compile error, and the generated code involves no reflection at runtime. Koin is a runtime service locator with a Kotlin DSL; resolution happens when `get()` / `inject()` is called, so a missing definition crashes there. Module verification tests bring that check back into CI.

questions.question: You are building a memory cache for decoded bitmaps. Which design is the soundest?
options: A ConcurrentHashMap without any eviction, cleared completely only when the app receives a low-memory warning
A map of WeakReferences only, so the garbage collector decides when to free bitmaps and no size limit is needed
A LinkedHashMap in insertion order bounded to 100 entries, so the oldest bitmaps are always evicted first
A LinkedHashMap in access order, bounded by total bytes (e.g. `allocationByteCount`), trimmed on `onTrimMemory` callbacks
questions.explanation: Access order gives true LRU, and bytes are the right unit because a full-screen bitmap can be hundreds of times larger than a thumbnail. Responding to trim callbacks gives memory back when the system is under pressure (iOS caches like NSCache react to memory warnings similarly). Weak-only caches are cleared on almost every GC, so the hit rate is poor; Coil uses a strong LRU with weak references only as a secondary layer.

questions.question: You write an OkHttp interceptor that retries failed requests. Which rules should it follow? Select all that apply.
options: Use Thread.sleep for backoff without concern, since interceptors always run on the main thread
Call `chain.proceed()` twice without closing the first response, since OkHttp closes it automatically
Honour a Retry-After header on 429 or 503 and cap the number of attempts with backoff
Only retry idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE) automatically, or requests that carry an idempotency key
Close the previous response before calling `chain.proceed()` again, otherwise OkHttp throws an IllegalStateException
questions.explanation: OkHttp requires that a response is closed before the chain can be used again, or it fails with an error about the previous response still being open. Automatic retries of non-idempotent POSTs can duplicate side effects. Interceptors run on the calling thread for `execute()` or on OkHttp's dispatcher threads for `enqueue()`, never necessarily the main thread, and a sleeping interceptor holds that thread for the whole wait.
